reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: A three-dimensional deformity combining lateral curvature and vertebral rotation, most commonly adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in otherwise healthy children, predominantly girls
It is often painless and detected as asymmetry of the shoulders, waist, or scapulae; a rib hump on the forward-bending (Adam's) test reflects the rotational component
Curve magnitude is quantified by the Cobb angle on a standing radiograph, and skeletal maturity (e.g. Risser sign) helps predict the risk of progression
Significant back pain, a rapidly progressive curve, an atypical (e.g. left thoracic) curve, or neurological signs should prompt a search for an underlying cause and MRI
Scoliosis may be idiopathic, congenital (vertebral anomalies), or neuromuscular (e.g. cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy), and management differs accordingly
Small curves are observed, moderate curves in a growing child may be braced to limit progression, and large or progressive curves are considered for surgical correction and fusion
The likelihood of progression is greatest during the adolescent growth spurt, so monitoring is intensified during rapid growth
Severe thoracic curves can restrict pulmonary function, an important consideration in early-onset and neuromuscular disease
reference.pathophysiology: Scoliosis is a structural lateral deviation of the spine accompanied by rotation of the vertebrae, which produces the characteristic rib or paravertebral prominence. In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis the cause is unknown but multifactorial, with genetic, growth-related, and neuromuscular balance factors implicated, and the deformity tends to worsen during periods of rapid skeletal growth. Congenital scoliosis results from failures of vertebral formation or segmentation present from birth, while neuromuscular scoliosis arises from asymmetrical muscle forces acting on the growing spine in conditions such as cerebral palsy. Progressive rotation and wedging of vertebrae make the curve increasingly rigid, and large thoracic curves can distort the chest and compromise lung capacity.
additionalDifferentials: Postural (non-structural) scoliosis that corrects on forward bending
Neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy)
Intraspinal pathology (syrinx, tethered cord, tumour) causing an atypical or painful curve
additionalInvestigations: Standing posteroanterior and lateral spinal radiographs to measure the Cobb angle and assess balance
Assessment of skeletal maturity (e.g. Risser sign, hand/wrist bone age)
Forward-bending (Adam's) test with a scoliometer to gauge rotation
MRI of the whole spine for atypical, painful, rapidly progressive, or early-onset curves, or when there are neurological signs
Pulmonary function testing for large thoracic or neuromuscular curves
redFlags: Neurological signs or symptoms suggesting an intraspinal cause requiring MRI
Significant or persistent back pain, unusual for idiopathic scoliosis
Rapid curve progression or an atypical curve pattern (e.g. left thoracic)
Respiratory compromise from a severe thoracic curve
reference.prognosis: Most mild adolescent idiopathic curves remain stable and require only monitoring, and bracing can prevent progression of moderate curves during growth; large or progressive curves may need surgical correction, and untreated severe curves can cause deformity, back pain, and in extreme thoracic cases cardiopulmonary compromise, while neuromuscular and congenital curves tend to be more progressive.
pitfalls: Assuming all scoliosis is benign idiopathic disease and missing an underlying intraspinal or neuromuscular cause
Overlooking a painful or atypical curve that warrants MRI
Failing to monitor closely during the adolescent growth spurt when progression is most likely
Confusing a compensatory postural curve from leg-length discrepancy with structural scoliosis
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Observe small curves with periodic clinical and radiographic monitoring of the Cobb angle throughout growth
Fit a spinal orthosis (brace) for moderate curves in the skeletally immature to limit progression
Refer progressive or large curves for surgical correction and spinal fusion, or growth-friendly instrumentation in early-onset disease
Investigate atypical, painful, rapidly progressive, or neurological presentations with whole-spine MRI to identify an underlying cause
Manage the underlying condition in congenital vertebral-anomaly and neuromuscular scoliosis, tailoring treatment accordingly
Monitor and support respiratory function in large thoracic and neuromuscular curves
Provide physiotherapy and multidisciplinary orthopaedic care, with neuromuscular input where relevant
